system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2144-05-12 15:35:00 to 2144-05-18 18:09:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with sickle cell disease Hb-SS and a history of osteosarcoma was admitted for persistent abdominal pain and constipation, initially thought to be related to proctitis. Imaging revealed a rectal mass with extensive lymphadenopathy, prompting a flexible sigmoidoscopy that identified a 1 cm abnormal mucosal area; biopsy confirmed poorly differentiated rectal adenocarcinoma. Staging with PET and MRI showed metastatic disease (T4B, N2, M1). She developed intermittent rectal bleeding requiring two units of packed red blood cells. Cancer-related pain was managed by initiating long-acting morphine, while her home Dilaudid was continued for breakthrough pain. Hydroxyurea was held due to thrombocytopenia. A port was placed and a CT-guided pelvic lymph node biopsy performed for tissue confirmation; results were pending at discharge. She was discharged home with a plan to follow up in the multidisciplinary rectal cancer clinic for chemotherapy initiation.
problems: Secondary and unspecified malignant neoplasm of intrapelvic lymph nodes
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of bone

Discharge Instructions:
Dear ___, 

You were admitted to the hospital after a diverting laparoscopic 
colostomy for surgical management of your large bowel 
obstruction. You have recovered from this procedure well and you 
are now ready to return home. 

You have a new colostomy. It is important to monitor the output 
from this stoma. It is expected that the stool from this ostomy 
will be solid and formed like regular stool. You should have ___ 
bowel movements daily. If you notice that you have not had any 
stool from your stoma in ___ days, please call the office. You 
may take an over the counter stool softener such as Colace if 
you find that you are becoming constipated. Please watch the 
appearance of the stoma (intestine that protrudes outside of 
your abdomen), it should be beefy red/pink, if you notice that 
the stoma is turning darker blue or purple, or dark red please 
call the office for advice. The stoma may ooze small amounts of 
blood at times when touched but this will improve over time. The 
skin around the ostomy site should be kept clean and intact. 
Monitor the skin around the stoma for any bulging or signs of 
infection listed above. Please care for the ostomy as you have 
been instructed by the ostomy nurses. ___ the skin around 
the stoma for any bulging or signs of infection listed above. 
You will be able to make an appointment with the ostomy nurse in 
the clinic ___ weeks after surgery. Please call the ostomy 
nurses clinic number which is listed in the ileostomy/colostomy 
handout packet given to you by the nursing staff. You will also 
have a visiting nurse at home for the next few weeks to help 
monitor your ostomy until you are comfortable caring for it on 
your own.

If you have any of the following symptoms please call the office 
at ___:
fever greater than 101.5
increasing abdominal distension
increasing abdominal pain
nausea/vomiting
inability to tolerate food or liquids
prolonged loose stool
extended constipation
inability to urinate

Incisions:
You have ___ laparoscopic surgical incisions on your abdomen 
which are closed with internal sutures.  It is important that 
you monitor these areas for signs and symptoms of infection 
including: increasing redness of the incision lines, 
white/green/yellow/malodorous drainage, increased pain at the 
incision, increased warmth of the skin at the incision, or 
swelling of the area.
You may shower; pat the incisions dry with a towel, do not rub.  
If you have steri-strips (the small white strips), they will 
fall off over time, please do not remove them. Please do not 
take a bath or swim until cleared by the surgical team.

Pain
It is expected that you will have pain after surgery, this will 
gradually improve over the first week or so you are home.  You 
should continue to take 2 Extra Strength Tylenol (___) for 
pain every 8 hours around the clock. Please do not take more 
than 3000mg of Tylenol in 24 hours or any other medications that 
contain Tylenol such as cold medication. Do not drink alcohol 
while taking Tylenol.  You may also take Advil (Ibuprofen) 600mg 
every 8 hours for 7 days, please take Advil with food. If these 
medications are not controlling your pain to a point where you 
can ambulate and perform minor tasks, you should take a dose of 
the narcotic pain medication MS contin.  Please do not take 
sedating medications or drink alcohol while taking the narcotic 
pain medication. Do not drive while taking narcotic medications.

Please note, palliative care also recommended a taper to your MS 
___ dose given possible withdrawal symptoms. They recommended 
starting at 60 mg three times a day and weaning with your 
outpatient provider from there. As discussed during your 
admission you may experience symptoms without weaning, this is 
at your discretion.

Activity
You may feel weak or ""washed out"" for up to 6 weeks after 
surgery. Do not lift greater than a gallon of milk for 3 weeks. 
At your post op appointment, your surgical team will clear you 
for heavier exercise.  In the meantime, you may climb stairs, 
and go outside and walk.  Please avoid traveling long distances 
until you speak with your surgical team at your post-op visit.  
Again, please do not drive while taking narcotic pain 
medications. 

Thank you for allowing us to participate in your care, we wish 
you all the best!

You have a new colostomy. It is important to monitor the output 
from this stoma. It is expected that the stool from this ostomy 
will be solid and formed like regular stool. You should have ___ 
bowel movements daily. If you notice that you have not had any 
stool from your stoma in ___ days, please call the office. You 
may take an over the counter stool softener such as Colace if 
you find that you are becoming constipated. Please watch the 
appearance of the stoma (intestine that protrudes outside of 
your abdomen), it should be beefy red/pink, if you notice that 
the stoma is turning darker blue or purple, or dark red please 
call the office for advice. The stoma may ooze small amounts of 
blood at times when touched but this will improve over time. The 
skin around the ostomy site should be kept clean and intact. 
Monitor the skin around the stoma for any bulging or signs of 
infection listed above. Please care for the ostomy as you have 
been instructed by the ostomy nurses. ___ the skin around 
the stoma for any bulging or signs of infection listed above. 
You will be able to make an appointment with the ostomy nurse in 
the clinic ___ weeks after surgery. Please call the ostomy 
nurses clinic number which is listed in the ileostomy/colostomy 
handout packet given to you by the nursing staff. You will also 
have a visiting nurse at home for the next few weeks to help 
monitor your ostomy until you are comfortable caring for it on 
your own.

If you have any of the following symptoms please call the office 
at ___:
fever greater than 101.5
increasing abdominal distension
increasing abdominal pain
nausea/vomiting
inability to tolerate food or liquids
prolonged loose stool
extended constipation
inability to urinate

Incisions:
You have ___ laparoscopic surgical incisions on your abdomen 
which are closed with internal sutures.  It is important that 
you monitor these areas for signs and symptoms of infection 
including: increasing redness of the incision lines, 
white/green/yellow/malodorous drainage, increased pain at the 
incision, increased warmth of the skin at the incision, or 
swelling of the area.
You may shower; pat the incisions dry with a towel, do not rub.  
If you have steri-strips (the small white strips), they will 
fall off over time, please do not remove them. Please do not 
take a bath or swim until cleared by the surgical team.

Pain
It is expected that you will have pain after surgery, this will 
gradually improve over the first week or so you are home.  You 
should continue to take 2 Extra Strength Tylenol (___) for 
pain every 8 hours around the clock. Please do not take more 
than 3000mg of Tylenol in 24 hours or any other medications that 
contain Tylenol such as cold medication. Do not drink alcohol 
while taking Tylenol.  You may also take Advil (Ibuprofen) 600mg 
every 8 hours for 7 days, please take Advil with food. If these 
medications are not controlling your pain to a point where you 
can ambulate and perform minor tasks, you should take a dose of 
the narcotic pain medication MS contin.  Please do not take 
sedating medications or drink alcohol while taking the narcotic 
pain medication. Do not drive while taking narcotic medications.

Please note, palliative care also recommended a taper to your MS 
___ dose given possible withdrawal symptoms. They recommended 
starting at 60 mg three times a day and weaning with your 
outpatient provider from there. As discussed during your 
admission you may experience symptoms without weaning, this is 
at your discretion.

Activity
You may feel weak or ""washed out"" for up to 6 weeks after 
surgery. Do not lift greater than a gallon of milk for 3 weeks. 
At your post op appointment, your surgical team will clear you 
for heavier exercise.  In the meantime, you may climb stairs, 
and go outside and walk.  Please avoid traveling long distances 
until you speak with your surgical team at your post-op visit.  
Again, please do not drive while taking narcotic pain 
medications. 

Thank you for allowing us to participate in your care, we wish 
you all the best!

TECHNIQUE:  Single phase split bolus contrast: MDCT axial images were acquired
through the abdomen and pelvis following intravenous contrast administration
with split bolus technique.
Oral contrast was not administered.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and reviewed on PACS.

DOSE:  Acquisition sequence:
   1) Stationary Acquisition 2.0 s, 0.5 cm; CTDIvol = 9.6 mGy (Body) DLP = 4.8
mGy-cm.
   2) Spiral Acquisition 5.9 s, 46.1 cm; CTDIvol = 8.7 mGy (Body) DLP = 400.2
mGy-cm.
 Total DLP (Body) = 405 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis ___

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST: Mild bibasilar atelectasis.  Otherwise, visualized lung fields
are unremarkable.  There is no evidence of pleural or pericardial effusion.

ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY: Ill-defined 1.0 cm hypodensity in the right hepatic lobe is
indeterminate, not definitively seen on the prior study.  The liver otherwise
demonstrates homogenous attenuation throughout.  There is no evidence of focal
lesions.  There is no evidence of intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary
dilatation.  The gallbladder is surgically absent.

PANCREAS: The pancreas has normal attenuation throughout, without evidence of
focal lesions or pancreatic ductal dilatation.  There is no peripancreatic
stranding.

SPLEEN: The spleen is not visualized.

ADRENALS: The right and left adrenal glands are normal in size and shape.

URINARY: Lobular contour of both kidneys is again seen with cortical scarring
similar to prior, likely sequela of prior infarctions.  Subcentimeter
hypodensity in the interpolar region of the left kidney is too small to
characterize, likely a cyst.  There is no hydronephrosis.  There is no
perinephric abnormality.

GASTROINTESTINAL: The stomach is unremarkable.  Small bowel loops demonstrate
normal caliber, wall thickness, and enhancement throughout.  Diffusely dilated
loops of large bowel measure up to 7.4 cm in the ascending colon and 4.8 cm in
the descending colon.  Apparent eccentric wall thickening as well as
perirectal inflammatory changes appear grossly similar to prior.  The appendix
is not visualized.

PELVIS: The urinary bladder and distal ureters are unremarkable.  There is no
definite free fluid in the pelvis.

REPRODUCTIVE ORGANS: The uterus is unremarkable.  No adnexal abnormality is
seen.

LYMPH NODES: Multiple enlarged nodes along the left pelvic sidewall appear
grossly similar, although retroperitoneal nodes, specifically at the left
para-aortic stations have increased in size, measuring up to 1.5 cm,
previously up to 1.0 cm.  An enlarged 1.2 cm retrocrural node sees (02:15) is
new.  Necrotic lymphadenopathy adjacent to the left psoas muscle is grossly
unchanged.  There is no mesenteric or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

VASCULAR: There is no abdominal aortic aneurysm.  Mild atherosclerotic disease
is noted.

BONES: There is no evidence of worrisome osseous lesions or acute fracture. 
Mixed lytic and lytic appearance of the bones are reflective of sickle cell
disease and scattered bone infarction.  Chronic bony changes with endplate
irregularities throughout the thoracolumbar spine are unchanged.  Serpentine
sclerosis at the bilateral femoral heads appears similar, concerning for
avascular necrosis.  No articular surface collapse.

SOFT TISSUES: The abdominal and pelvic wall is within normal limits.

IMPRESSION:


-Findings concerning for large bowel obstruction, likely due to known rectal
cancer
-Interval increase in retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy is concerning for
disease progression.

NOTIFICATION:  Updated findings with ___ at 09:13 on ___.

EXAMINATION:  FL GASTROGRAFIN ENEMA

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with CRC and now CT w/ large bowel
obstruction// assess degree of stenosis?

TECHNIQUE:  AP and lateral scout views were obtained.  A rectal tube was
inserted and 60cc of water soluble contrast was administered via gravity past
the level of stricture in the sigmoid colon.  Spot views were obtained.

DOSE:  Acc air kerma: 20.1 mGy; Accum DAP: 473.8 uGym2; Fluoro time: 01:02
minutes

COMPARISON:  CT dated ___

FINDINGS: 

After scout images were obtained, a rectal tube was inserted into the
rectum. 60 cc of water soluble contrast was administered via gravity.

Contrast is seen filling the rectum, and passing through a high-grade stenosis
in the rectosigmoid, to opacify the distal sigmoid colon.

High-grade stenosis of the rectosigmoid colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. I understand you've been having some abdominal pain and trouble passing gas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started a few days ago. I haven’t passed gas in three days, and my belly is really bloated. I’ve been trying to eat, but I just feel full all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you recently started chemotherapy for your rectal cancer. Has anything changed since then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The bleeding stopped, and I was going to the bathroom normally at first. But now this—no solid stools, just a little liquid now and then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We did a CT scan this morning, and it shows your colon is dilated up to the rectum. That suggests a blockage, likely from your known cancer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A blockage? So that’s why I can’t pass anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The scan also shows the lymph nodes around your abdomen have gotten larger, which may mean the cancer is progressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I was hoping the chemo would slow it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re going to transfer you to the colorectal surgery team to discuss options for relieving the blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did a gastrograffin enema yesterday, and it confirmed a high-grade narrowing in your rectosigmoid colon. That’s what’s causing the obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now? Can they fix it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your metastatic cancer, we can’t remove the tumor. But we can create a colostomy—a new opening for stool to leave your body—so the blockage is bypassed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A colostomy? Like a bag on my belly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It’s a loop colostomy, temporary for now. It will let your bowel rest and prevent further blockage. You’ll get teaching from the ostomy nurse while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I have to live with it forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Right now, the goal is to relieve the obstruction and get you comfortable. We’ll discuss long-term options with your oncology team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… when would this happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling it for tomorrow morning. It’s a laparoscopic procedure, so recovery should be quicker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from surgery. You did great—the colostomy was placed successfully. You have three small incisions on your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How does it look? Is it working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stoma is pink and moist, which is good. It’s already starting to drain—normal sign. The ostomy nurse will check on you soon to help with care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on pain meds, but I feel okay. Will I stay here a few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep you for a few days to monitor your recovery, make sure you’re eating, and that the colostomy is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood—wasn’t it low before surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin was low, so you got two units of blood before surgery. We’re watching it daily. No further drops so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I passed gas through the stoma, and I had a bowel movement into the bag. It felt good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’re going to start you on a regular diet today. Keep drinking fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pain meds? I’m on Dilaudid now, but I usually take MS Contin at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Palliative care reviewed your case. Because you’re on high-dose opioids, we’re switching you to 60 mg MS Contin three times a day to avoid withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried about that. Can I go back to my normal dose later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll taper it slowly with your outpatient provider. It’s safer this way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my chemo? I was supposed to get another cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We talked to your oncologist. They want to see you this week to decide when to restart FOLFOX.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’re eating, the colostomy is working, and you’re walking around. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Will I have help at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a visiting nurse will come to check your stoma and incisions. You’ll also have an appointment with the ostomy nurse in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for that means something’s wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you have fever over 101.5, severe pain, no output from the stoma for two days, or if the stoma turns dark red or purple.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the incisions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep them clean and dry. Watch for redness, swelling, or pus. You can shower, but no baths or swimming yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain-wise, I’m on Tylenol. Can I take ibuprofen too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can take 600 mg ibuprofen every 8 hours with food for a week. But don’t exceed 3000 mg of Tylenol in 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the MS Contin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it if the other meds don’t control your pain. But don’t drive or drink alcohol while on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: you’re passing stool, eating well, and your labs look stable. We’re clearing you for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about managing the colostomy alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The visiting nurse will help until you’re confident. And the ostomy nurse is just a call away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready, just a little overwhelmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely normal. You’ve been through a lot. We’re here for you every step of the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your discharge orders are ready. You’ll go home with a visiting nurse, and your follow-up is in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take MS Contin 60 mg every 8 hours, Tylenol for mild pain, Miralax daily, and a daily Lovenox shot to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help with the shot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The visiting nurse will give the first few doses. They’ll teach your sister how to do it if she’s willing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She is. That helps a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just take it slow, rest, and call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with metastatic rectal cancer and sickle cell disease was admitted for right lower quadrant pain and obstipation. Imaging revealed a large bowel obstruction due to her known rectal cancer, with interval increase in retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy suggesting disease progression. She underwent a laparoscopic diverting loop colostomy to relieve the obstruction. Preoperatively, she was transfused two units of packed red blood cells due to anemia. Postoperatively, she recovered well, was advanced to a regular diet, and tolerated the colostomy. Pain management was adjusted to prevent opioid withdrawal by transitioning to 60 mg MS Contin three times daily with a planned taper. She received ostomy education and was discharged home with visiting nurse services, a plan to resume chemotherapy, and follow-up in two weeks.
